newsitem.title: FINLAND: Nokia may cut Ericsson P/E gap - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Nokia may cut Ericsson P/E gap - analysts.

text.p: With last week's Q1 report from Swedish telecoms major Ericsson Ab spotlighting the role of mobile handsets, some analysts say shares in Finland's Nokia can benefit from a shift in sentiment.

Investors comparing the two traditionally focus on Nokia's relatively larger exposure to handset markets -- where margins are under clearest pressure -- versus Ericsson's strength in infrastructure and in fixed line markets, seen as more robust.
That has been one constant behind a valuation premium for Ericsson over Nokia of around eight-nine points in prospective price-earnings ratios.

But Ericsson, whose report on Friday for the first time enabled a breakdown between its mobile handsets and systems performance, highlighted the role of mobile handsets which had 100 percent sales growth, and said it gained market share.

Analysts said that growth came in booming digital markets, so Ericsson was more likely to have gained over the likes of Motorola than over Nokia, which at the end of last year rose to claim world leadership in digital handset markets.

"Handsets will be an increasing part of Ericsson -- it's starting to look more like Motorola and Nokia," said Lauri Rosendahl at Aros Securities. His theory is that this creates scope for the valuation gap between the two to narrow.

Nokia, which as Europe's number one in handset sales is growing from a much larger base, is not expected to put in as glitzy a growth figure as Ericsson's 100 percent when it reports on Tuesday, partly because it has a larger analogue share.
The median of a Reuters survey of analysts' forecasts for Nokia's pre-tax profit, due around 0900 GMT, is 1.26 billion markka, sharply up from 399 million in the year-ago period.
One analyst said he would be happy with 30 percent handset sales growth; another, citing particularly weak handset sales in Q1 1996, said he was looking for as much as a 60 percent improvement.

Trying to gauge the reaction of overseas investors to Nokia's report, Rosendahl said he expected their impression may be of an opposite picture than at Ericsson: slower handset growth and faster growth on the systems side.
"The market will be completely confused (by this)," he said. "Some will assume Ericsson is beating Nokia in handsets and Nokia is beating Ericsson in systems."

If the standard view on margin erosion in handsets prevails, that could point to Nokia gaining ground to close the valuation gap against Ericsson, although Rosendahl was not sure exactly when this might start to be priced in.
According to his estimates, Ericsson typically trades around 25-30 times 1997/98 per share earnings with Nokia at 17-20.
Other analysts agreed that, in terms of market perceptions especially abroad, the similarity between Ericsson and Nokia is growing. One saw scope for a sentiment shift towards Nokia.
But Jeremy Alun-Jones at Lehman Brothers in London put much of this down to Ericsson's new style of reporting.
Ericsson put in mobile systems growth of 22 percent, which some analysts found below expectations and which was cited as a reason behind its sharp fall in New York and Stockholm.

But Alun-Jones said unbundling both businesses, formerly grouped in "radio communications" which tended to show growth rates around 40 percent, was bound to show a lower percentage growth rate for systems, the larger chunk of the old division.
"I think Ericsson will maintain a considerable premium over Nokia," he said, citing the Swedish firm's solid record.
He agreed the current valuation gap -- which he had around nine points -- could narrow, but said it was very challenging to assume this may all come from gains in Nokia.
Nonetheless, on Monday at least Ericsson in Stockholm fell more sharply than Nokia in Helsinki, as both took a hit from Wall St's negative response to Ericsson's report.
In early afternoon trade, Nokia was down about 1.5 percent with Ericsson marked down nearer five percent.
